label: Qubit spectroscopy vs flux
axes: A 2-D color map of measured response amplitude: the horizontal axis is the applied flux bias swept across the qubit's flux line (a second, redundant top axis restates the same sweep in bias-source units), the vertical axis is the swept drive/probe frequency, and color encodes the response at each (bias, frequency) cell. Overlaid on the map are a dashed vertical line marking the chosen idle bias and one or two diamond markers naming the claimed sweet spot(s), captioned upper and/or lower. Some runs render one such map per qubit as a grid of small panels sharing this layout.
correct_signature: One continuous band of contrasting color runs across the whole bias sweep as a single-valued curve: for every bias column there is exactly one dominant frequency band, and it stays connected from column to neighbouring column rather than breaking into isolated patches.

The band bends smoothly and reverses direction once inside the sweep - it approaches from one side, flattens into a rounded turning point, and falls away on the other side, with the two flanks roughly mirroring each other about that turning point.
The band's contrast stands well clear of the background: its color excursion is several times the cell-to-cell scatter of the surrounding map, so the eye follows it without being told where to look.

The band keeps a roughly constant width along the sweep - it may thicken modestly on the flanks but never fans out to fill the frequency axis; its width relative to the swept range is a zoom choice and is not itself evidence but never fans out to fill the frequency axis.
The claimed sweet-spot marker sits ON the band, at the column where the band's slope changes sign - not part-way up a monotonic flank and not in the background.
If two markers (an upper and a lower extremum) are claimed, the band genuinely shows two turning points of opposite curvature within the sweep; a single arch supports only one such claim.
The idle-bias line crosses the band at the frequency the band actually occupies in that column, i.e. the overlay is drawn on the same structure the data shows.

failure_appearance.wrong_peak: A band is clearly visible, but the claimed marker is not at its turning point. Seen in the archive as: the marker parked part-way up a monotonic flank; the marker at the very first or last bias column where the band is still climbing; the marker sitting a band-width or more off the band, on an isolated bright cell of background speckle; or two markers claimed against a single arch, placed at different bias columns with no second turning point of opposite curvature between them.
failure_appearance.no_signal: The map is uniform speckle - random cell-to-cell mottling, sometimes organised into vertical per-column or horizontal per-row striping, with no band that persists across neighbouring bias columns at any frequency - yet upper and lower sweet-spot markers are still drawn on it. This is the most common failure in the archive: several whole runs and several individual panels of multi-qubit sheets show no band anywhere and still carry a full marker set.
failure_appearance.noisy: The band exists but only as a broad, ragged brightening: its width is comparable to its own vertical excursion across the sweep, its edges break up from column to column, and striping of comparable contrast crosses it, so the turning point cannot be placed to better than a good fraction of that excursion. Curvature is present but so shallow relative to the band's own width that the band reads as nearly straight. The single figure this family archives as node-accepted is of exactly this weak-contrast kind, so the accepted bar here is low.
failure_appearance.feature_present_fit_failed: A clean curved band is plainly drawn, but nothing on the overlay backs the numeric claim: the marker legend is present yet empty, or no diamond appears anywhere on the band, or a marker is parked in a corner of the frame well away from the band. The structure the claim is supposed to describe is visible and unannotated.

abstain_when: The swept bias range covers only a monotonic segment of the band - it rises or falls across the entire sweep with no turning point inside the frame. The picture can neither confirm nor refute an extremum that was never measured.
The band is visible but unresolved: it fills most of the frequency axis, or only a handful of bias columns spans the frame, so curvature and turning point are not determinable from the rendering.
The figure is a multi-panel sheet and it cannot be established which panel the numeric claim refers to - panels in the same sheet routinely range from clean arch to pure speckle.
Color mapping defeats the reading - the map is saturated or clipped so band and background cannot be distinguished, or the legend box covers the region where a marker would sit.
Two bands of comparable contrast cross or run parallel (a spurious mode or a neighbouring line) and the picture alone gives no reason to attribute one of them to the claimed qubit.
notes: Evidence is thin and asymmetric. Only ONE run in the archive is presented as node-accepted for this family, and it is a marginal example: a broad, weakly-curved band under heavy per-column striping, with two sweet-spot markers at different bias columns and no visually sharp turning point. Treat it as the floor of acceptability, not the model of it. The strongest correct-signature evidence comes from multi-qubit panel sheets in the same archive, where several panels show textbook arches (a bright band rising, flattening into a rounded top, and falling, with the marker on the apex) alongside sibling panels that are pure speckle - the same run, same sweep, same overlay code. NO node-rejected run is archived for this family, so every failure appearance above is read off panels the node did not flag rather than off a recorded rejection; the wrong_peak / no_signal / noisy / feature_present_fit_failed descriptions are all grounded in observed panels, but none carries a rejection label to confirm the node itself considers them failures. drifted is set to null: this family renders a single non-repeated 2-D sweep, so a slow time drift has no repeated trace to shift against, and no discontinuous step or offset in a band was observed in any figure read - do not fill this in without a real example. Critically for the judge: this node draws sweet-spot markers unconditionally. Markers are present, labelled, and numerically confident on maps that contain no signal whatsoever, so the presence of a marker is worth nothing as evidence - only whether it lands on a real band's turning point. The feature is a ridge in a 2-D map, not a peak on one axis, so the localizer is none: judge by whole-figure signature trust, never by pointing at a coordinate. Also note the redundant top axis restating the same bias sweep in source units - it is not a second independent variable, and a claim must not be checked against it as though it were.
